title: 15.2 A 1024-Channel 0.00029mm2/ch 74nW/ch Online Spatial Spike-Sorting Chip with Event-Driven Spike Detection and Self-Organizing Map Clustering
problem: High-density multi-electrode arrays (HD-MEA) for brain-computer interfaces generate massive raw spike data that must be reduced on-chip for wireless operation. Prior spike-sorting (SS) designs either require large input buffers, use temporal features that don't scale to multi-channel systems, access entire clustering memory per spike, or consume high power and area.
motivation: Next-gen BCIs require high-channel-count HD-MEA for fine motor/speech decoding and brain understanding, but raw data rates are prohibitive for wireless transmission without on-chip sorting.
method: The chip detects spikes (sudden electrical pulses from neurons) only when they actually occur—event-driven detection—rather than continuously reading all raw data, which saves memory and power. Instead of using spike timing to sort them (which fails with many channels), it uses waveform shape—the electrical fingerprint of each neuron—to group similar spikes, which is spatial spike-sorting. It organizes these groupings using a self-organizing map, a technique that learns from each new spike without storing all previous data in memory. Processing only real events, sorting by fingerprint shape, and avoiding per-spike full-memory access lets the chip handle 1024 channels with sub-50-microsecond latency.
key_novelty: Combining event-driven spike detection (processing only real neural signals), spatial spike-sorting (grouping by waveform fingerprint), and self-organizing map clustering enables a chip to handle 1024 neural signal channels with low power consumption and sub-50-microsecond response time.
contributions: Event-driven spike detection avoiding large sample buffers
Spatial spike-sorting using waveform features vs. temporal features
Self-organizing map (SOM) clustering with efficient memory access
